Custom evaluators

Let users author their own eval judge — name, prompt, scoring — optionally starting from a built-in.

Status: Design prototype (frontend/designer scope). Custom evaluators live in memory only — no API, no persistence. Built-in evaluators still come from the backend unchanged, and no backend contract for authoring exists yet.
Living document — how to keep this file updated (maintenance contract)

This file is the source of truth for the Custom evaluators prototype and is the only context a future session reads when resuming this feature. Keep it in sync with the build: whenever behavior changes, reflect it in the relevant section — Main changes, Behaviour, or Edge cases.

Four rules:

  1. Record the final result, not the journey. Capture only where a value or behavior landed — never intermediate steps (a font size that went 12 → 14 → 16 is "16").
  2. Write for a PM. Every section is concise and plain-language, so a PM can derive user stories from it. There are no separate technical sections — no data model, backend contract, or code-integration lists.
  3. Keep it concise — no useless verbosity. Lead with the fact; one idea per sentence; bullets and tables over prose; name concrete values (not "a sensible cap"); cut filler ("simply", "essentially", hedges); never restate. If deleting a sentence loses no information a reader needs, delete it.
  4. Remove, don't strike through. When a behavior is dropped, delete its entry and its screenshot — don't keep a changelog.

Keep it minimal. This doc has exactly three content sections — Main changes, Behaviour, Edge cases — plus screenshots. Don't add data-model, backend, or code-integration sections; that detail belongs in the code, not here.

Screenshots. Store in ft_custom_evaluators_assets/ and embed by relative path under the relevant Behaviour subsection. Keep them current — retake and replace the file in place when the UI changes materially; don't accumulate old versions. Use a <div class="todo"> placeholder when a shot can't be captured yet.

Main changes

  • The Eval Definitions tab was read-only. It now has a Custom section below the built-in category groups where users author their own evaluators.
  • The New evaluator button in the tab header is the only way to create one.
  • A create/edit modal captures type, name, description, the scoring logic — a judge prompt or code — and scoring.
  • Evaluator type — the first choice in the modal: LLM as a judge (a prompt graded by a model) or Code (a script that returns the score).
  • A code evaluator's logic is either written in the modal in a JavaScript editor, or taken from an existing workspace function.
  • A code evaluator's Pass threshold enables itself only when the logic returns a number. Code that returns a pass/fail verdict or a label gets the field greyed out, with a line saying why — the modal works this out from the code, so nothing is asked of the author.
  • Start from a template — an optional picker in the modal that prefills the whole form from any built-in judge, so users adjust rather than write from scratch.
  • Three scoring modes: Numeric 0–1 with a pass threshold, Binary pass/fail, or Enum — an author-defined list of values the judge returns.
  • Enum evaluators set How many values the judge returns — exactly one, or one or more. One-or-more adds a pass rule that turns several returned values into a single verdict.
  • Custom cards get a ⋮ menu — Details, Duplicate, Delete. Built-in cards are unchanged and stay read-only.
  • Custom evaluators appear in the evaluator picker when launching an experiment, so they can actually be run.

Behaviour

Where custom evaluators live

The Evaluators tab groups evaluators by category — General Quality, RAG, Code / Deterministic. Custom is a fourth group, always last.

The Custom group is hidden entirely until the workflow has at least one custom evaluator — a fresh workflow shows only the built-in groups. Creating the first one makes the group appear.

Picking the evaluator type

The first control in the modal is a two-option segmented control — LLM as a judge (default) or Code. It decides what the rest of the form asks for:

LLM as a judgeCode
LogicAn Instructions promptJavaScript — written in the modal or taken from a workspace function
ScoringNumeric, Binary or EnumNot a choice — derived from what the logic returns
Start from a templateAvailableHidden

The type is editable after creation — an evaluator can be switched either way. The card's type chip reads LLM as a judge or Code.

Creating an evaluator from scratch

The modal asks for five things, in order: the type, an optional template, a name, an optional description, and the logic — then the scoring.

The instructions field is the judge prompt sent to the model for every test-case output. It's a tall autosizing textarea, since these run long.

Writing a code evaluator

A Code radio pair picks where the logic lives: Write it here (default) or Use a workspace function.

  • Write it here — a JavaScript editor, seeded with a commented evaluate({ input, actualOutput, expectedOutput, context }) function. It returns a number between 0 and 1 to score the output, or true/false to pass or fail it outright.
  • Use a workspace function — a searchable picker listing every reusable function in the workspace. The card then shows a Function: … chip.

Either way there's no scoring control — a code evaluator's scoring comes from what its logic returns, not from a choice in the form.

When a code evaluator gets a pass threshold

A threshold only means something when there's a number to compare it against, so the field enables itself based on what the logic returns. The author is never asked to declare it.

Write it hereUse a workspace function
What's readThe return statements, re-read each time the editor loses focusThe output type the function declares
Threshold enabledA number — 0.8, raw / 10, similarity(a, b), a === b ? 1 : 0INTEGER, FLOAT or CURRENCY
Threshold disabledA verdict — true, score >= 0.7, !bad, 'grounded'Anything else it declares — true/false, text, a fixed set of values, an object, a date

Disabled means greyed out and left in place, not hidden, with a line underneath saying why — "Your code returns a pass or fail verdict, not a score". For a function the line names the declared type instead. The field also loses its required marker, so a verdict-returning evaluator saves without it.

Both columns follow one rule: the threshold is only taken away on positive evidence that the result isn't a number. The two read different things because a declared type is a closed list of possibilities while JavaScript source isn't — code the modal can't read keeps its threshold, exactly as an undeclared output type does.

A code evaluator whose threshold is switched off is saved as a Binary one, so its card, its results column and the experiment launch form all leave the threshold out.

TODO screenshot → ft_custom_evaluators_assets/modal-code-function.png: the Code tab set to Use a workspace function with a function picked — ideally one declaring a BOOLEAN output, so the threshold is greyed out with the declared-type line.

Starting from a template

Picking a built-in under Start from a template fills the form in one step: the name becomes <Built-in> (copy), and description, instructions and scoring are copied over. Everything stays editable.

Only built-in judges are listed — a built-in code evaluator keeps its logic on the backend, so there'd be nothing to copy.

Changing the template again re-fills the form. The picker only appears when creating — not when editing.

TODO screenshot → ft_custom_evaluators_assets/modal-from-template.png: the modal prefilled from the RAG Groundedness template — name, description, judge prompt and scoring all filled in.

Choosing how it scores

A three-option segmented control sets the scoring mode:

  • Numeric 0–1 (default) — a Pass threshold field appears below, defaulting to 0.7. Outputs scoring below it count as a failure.
  • Binary pass/fail — nothing to configure.
  • Enum — a How many values the judge returns control and a Values editor appear. Each value row has a Counts as pass checkbox. Starts with two blank rows; Add value appends more, and the trash button removes a row (disabled at two rows).

Only Numeric evaluators carry a threshold. Binary and Enum ones decide pass/fail themselves, so no threshold field appears in the modal or in the experiment launch form.

TODO screenshot → ft_custom_evaluators_assets/modal-binary.png: the modal with Binary pass/fail scoring selected and no Pass threshold field.

How many values an enum judge returns

Above the Values editor, How many values the judge returns is a pair of radios side by side: Exactly one (default) or One or more. Every label in this section is phrased around what the judge returns, so the per-value Counts as pass checkbox can't be mistaken for the verdict rule.

  • Exactly one — the judge answers with a single value. It passes when that value is marked Counts as pass. Nothing else to configure.
  • One or more — the judge may answer with several, so a rule appears below the values, labelled The test case passes when the judge returns: Only pass values (default, strict — one non-pass value fails the case) or At least one pass value (lenient).

The Counts as pass checkbox means the same thing in both modes — only the rule for combining several values changes. Switching back to Exactly one hides the rule and drops it from the saved evaluator.

What an enum evaluator looks like on its card

Enum cards show Scoring: Enum plus a values chip listing the values in author order, in place of the Pass Threshold chip. The chip reads Values: … for single-select and Values (multi-select): … when the judge may return several.

Editing, duplicating and deleting

Custom cards carry a ⋮ menu next to their type chip. Built-in cards don't.

  • Details — reopens the modal on that evaluator, with the template picker hidden.
  • Duplicate — opens a create modal prefilled from it, named <Name> (copy).
  • Delete — asks for confirmation first, then removes the card.
TODO screenshot → ft_custom_evaluators_assets/card-menu.png: a saved custom evaluator card with its ⋮ menu open, showing Details, Duplicate and Delete.

Running an experiment with one

Custom evaluators show up in the evaluator picker on Run New Experiment, grouped under a Custom heading alongside the built-in groups. From there they behave like any other evaluator — selectable, and their threshold is editable per experiment.

Built-in code evaluators ask for response-schema paths in that form. A custom code evaluator doesn't — its code gets the whole test case, so no paths block appears for it.

Edge cases

  • In-memory only — custom evaluators are lost on page refresh. Nothing is saved to a backend; this is the main prototype limitation.
  • Duplicate names are blocked — saving a name that matches any evaluator, built-in or custom, shows an inline error instead of saving. The check ignores case and the evaluator being edited.
  • Template prompts are mocked — the backend doesn't return instruction text for built-ins. A few well-known evaluators have hand-written prompts; the rest get one generated from their name, description and scoring mode. Real templates need a backend field.
  • Binary evaluators have no threshold — switching to Binary drops the field entirely, and a threshold chip never appears on the card.
  • Enum needs two distinct values and one pass — saving is blocked with an inline error when fewer than two values are filled in, when two values match (case-insensitively), or when no value is marked as a pass. This holds however many values the judge returns: an enum with no pass value could never pass. Values are capped at 50 characters.
  • Switching evaluator type keeps what you typed — the judge prompt, the code and the picked function all survive a switch away and back, but only the active type's logic is saved: a code evaluator carries no instructions, and a judge carries no code.
  • Code evaluators never choose a scoring mode — the segmented control is hidden, and the mode lands on Numeric or Binary according to what the logic returns, whatever was selected before switching to Code.
  • Unreadable logic keeps its threshold — code the modal can't classify, a function with no declared output type, and a function declaring several output values all leave the field enabled. Guessing wrong and taking a threshold away from an author who needs it is worse than leaving one they can ignore.
  • The check runs on blur, not per keystroke — the threshold doesn't flicker mid-edit. Comments are ignored, so a commented-out return true doesn't count, and a ternary is judged on its branches rather than its condition — a === b ? 1 : 0 returns a number despite the comparison.
  • Workspace functions are barely validated — the declared output type decides whether a threshold applies, but nothing checks the function's signature or that a numeric one stays within 0–1, and the picker lists Python functions alongside JavaScript ones. Deleting the function afterwards isn't tracked either.
  • Code isn't executed — nothing runs or lints the script in the prototype; the editor is a JavaScript editor with syntax highlighting only.
  • Switching scoring mode keeps what you typed — the enum rows, the selection, the pass rule and the threshold all survive a switch away and back; only the active mode's field is validated on save.
  • The pass rule is only saved for multi-select — a single-select enum carries no rule. Toggling how many values the judge returns back and forth keeps the rule you picked while the modal is open, but an evaluator saved as single-select reopens on the default rule.
  • Built-ins are never Enum — starting from a template always lands on Numeric or Binary. Only Duplicate of a custom enum evaluator copies its values, selection and pass rule across.
  • Custom evaluators are never filtered out by node type — the experiment picker hides RAG evaluators for non-RAG nodes and Code evaluators for reply nodes, but the Custom group always shows. A custom evaluator that only makes sense for one node type is the author's responsibility.
  • Committed versions are read-only — on a committed application version the New evaluator button is disabled and the ⋮ menu actions are disabled. This matches datasets and experiments.
  • Deleting doesn't rewrite history — experiments already scored with a custom evaluator keep their results; the confirmation dialog says so.
